nameStory: The American Copper Underwing gets its name from a delightful surprise it reveals when it takes flight. While its forewings are perfectly camouflaged in mottled brown, its hindwings flash brilliant copper-orange markings that catch the light like polished pennies. This "underwing" pattern is a classic defense strategy—startling predators with a sudden burst of bright color when the moth opens its wings.
description: The American Copper Underwing is a medium-sized moth that's a master of disguise by day and a flashy showoff by night. With wings spanning about 1.5 to 2 inches across, it looks like a piece of weathered bark when resting with wings closed. But open those wings and you'll see white hindwings decorated with striking copper-orange patches and bold black lines. These sturdy moths are common summer visitors to porch lights and outdoor gatherings throughout New England.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern Contrast
idTips.description: Forewings are mottled brown and gray like tree bark, while hindwings are bright white with copper-orange patches and black crosslines—the contrast is dramatic when wings open

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a wingspan of 1.5-2 inches, robust body, and triangular forewings that fold tent-like over the body when at rest

idTips.label: Resting Posture
idTips.description: Sits with wings folded roof-like over body during day, pressed flat against tree bark where the mottled brown pattern provides perfect camouflage

idTips.label: Flight Behavior
idTips.description: Strong, direct flight pattern with flashing copper hindwings visible as bright pulses—often attracted to lights on warm summer evenings

idTips.label: Hindwing Details
idTips.description: White hindwings with coppery-orange coloring and distinct black crosslines that remain visible even when wings are partially closed

habitat: American Copper Underwings thrive in mixed woodlands, forest edges, and suburban areas throughout New England where broadleaf trees are abundant. You'll find them in oak-maple forests, along woodland trails, in parks with mature trees, and around homes with fruit trees or large shade trees. They're especially common where apple, oak, maple, and other deciduous trees grow, as these serve as host plants for their caterpillars.

seasonality.spring: Caterpillars are actively feeding on fresh tree leaves, appearing as green larvae with white stripes and a distinctive hump on their backs. Look for leaf-rolling damage on broadleaf trees where larvae pupate.
seasonality.summer: Newly emerged adults gather under loose bark in mid-summer, then become active at night from July onward. This is peak time to spot them at porch lights and outdoor lighting.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue flying through October, often seen at late-season flowers or artificial lights on warm evenings. Mated females are laying eggs that will overwinter.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs survive the cold months, tucked away on tree branches. No moths are visible, but next year's generation is waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: American Copper Underwings are surprisingly social for moths—dozens of newly emerged adults will huddle together under the same piece of loose bark like they're having a neighborhood block party before they start their nighttime adventures.
confusionNotes: Many brown moths look similar when wings are closed, but the copper underwing's bright white and orange hindwings are unmistakable when revealed. If you see flashing copper and white in flight, you've found your moth—most other 'underwing' species show different color combinations like red, yellow, or pink.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'underwing' refers to the hindwings that are normally hidden beneath the forewings when at rest. This dramatic color difference between fore and hind wings is called 'flash coloration'—a defense mechanism where sudden bright colors can startle predators long enough for the moth to escape.
compareHints: As the only Amphipyra species regularly found in New England, the American Copper Underwing is most easily confused with other noctueid moths of similar size. However, its distinctive white hindwings with copper-orange markings set it apart from relatives like the various Catocala underwing moths, which typically show red, pink, or yellow hindwing colors instead of the characteristic copper tone.
